Phidias. The preeminent sculptor of ancient Greece, directing the sculptural program of the Parthenon during Athens' Golden Age around 500 to 432 before the common era. His colossal chryselephantine—gold-and-ivory—statues of gods set the standard for monumental divine representation that influenced Western sculpture for millennia.

Phidias directed the overall artistic vision of the Parthenon from 447 to 432 before the common era, supervising the architectural sculptures including the pediments, metopes, and frieze. He designed the Athena Parthenos around 438 before the common era, a forty-foot-high chryselephantine statue housed within the Parthenon, renowned for its majesty and detailed ornamentation. He created the Statue of Zeus at Olympia around 435 before the common era, another gold-and-ivory colossus that became one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, whose description inspired awe for eight hundred years.

Phidias was a master of contrapposto and idealized human anatomy—his figures embodied the classical ideal of perfect proportion and heroic beauty. He established the sculptor as an intellectual leader equal to architects and philosophers, shaping Athenian cultural policy under Pericles. He fell victim to political persecution around 430 before the common era and likely died in exile, though his legacy outlasted his contemporaries and his Parthenon sculptures remain the pinnacle of classical sculptural achievement.
